set.v: Share of a bank haul, 'mostly gold and diamonds' (no sum)
set.tovw: Lead grade B (treasure thread): the local paper and the Grand Rapids Herald independently name the hill, the men and the digs; nothing found in three tries
pinev: Five Mile Hill crest, named in the 1900 Tribune; Baty's 90-ft shaft was sunk from the crest. Crest is the highest point of the dune mass south of the harbour on 2016 Michigan 1 m lidar (237.7 m).
'Just back of the summit' (Grand Rapids Herald 1900), i.e. the landward (east) side of the crest, within the 250 m ring.

tw-mi-grand-haven-light-house-hill-convi.st: The Grand Rapids Herald's fuller telling (1900): some forty years earlier officer Curtis W. Gray took a dying Jackson prisoner's confession that a gang had made a big bank haul, fled to the mouth of the Grand and split the loot. The man carried his share, 'mostly gold and diamonds', at dawn to 'the place where the light house stands, then turned into the woods' and buried it 'on the top of a little ridge of sandy soil … near the light house, overlooking the lake and river', drawing a chart; Gray dug shallow holes and found nothing. Baty, 'a mine owner and prospector', dug at 'the summit of the Five Mile hill' in 1899; in April 1900 he and his partner Robinson hired diggers at $1 a foot, reached 20 ft aiming for 60, and turned up a page of an 1879 Grand Rapids Eagle at about 20 ft. The spot was 'just back of the summit', reached by the river ridge through the woods.
tw-mi-grand-haven-light-house-hill-convi.t: An 1879 newspaper 20 ft down means the sand has moved: a shifting dune can bury a cache far deeper than it was laid, or carry it off the summit.
src: "Gold and Diamonds Repose under Five-Mile Hill at Grand Haven", Grand Rapids Herald, 23 Apr 1900, p. 2 (GenealogyBank)
